newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin meets PM, new budget battle looms.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin meets PM, new budget battle looms.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, back in the Kremlin after May Day holidays, met senior officials on Monday to discuss national security and economic reforms as his government prepared for battle over unpopular spending cuts.

In talks with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin focused on wage arrears -- Russia's number one social problem affecting millions of workers -- and on seeking parliamentary backing for austerity plans.

He also met Ivan Rybkin, secretary of the policy-making Security Council, to discuss Moscow's delicate relations with the breakaway region of Chechnya and the development of a new doctrine of national security.
He later formally welcomed King Juan Carlos of Spain at the start of a three-day royal visit.
The flurry of engagements followed a break for the 66-year-old president, first at the Black Sea resort of Sochi and then at a country residence outside Moscow.
Yeltsin is keen to keep up the momentum from his promotion of liberals to top government jobs in March.
Chernomyrdin was expected to try to persuade the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, on May 21 to accept spending cuts aimed at bridging a yawning gap between revenues and expenditure.
Mikhail Zadornov, head of the Duma's budget committee, said he had received the spending bill, which a government official said would cut about one fifth of the 1997 budget.

Zadornov told Reuters that deputies, who approved the original budget only after months of angry debate, might retaliate with calls to print money to keep spending on track. Yeltsin has vowed not to take such a course, which would reignite inflation.

Russia's budget gap has been an important concern for the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which suspended disbursing a $10 billion three-year loan because of low tax revenues. Officials say they expect payment to resume this month.
Chernomyrdin said he hoped the Duma, dominated by Yeltsin's communist foes, would show "a spirit of responsibility."

Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin also agreed that the prime minister should go to Ukraine on May 28-29 to help to patch up Russia's frayed relations with its Slav neighbour before a much-postponed visit to Kiev by Yeltsin himself, probably in June.
The Kremlin said the Security Council would meet on May 7 to discuss a new national security doctrine, widely seen as a prerequisite for a planned overhaul of the hard-up armed forces.

Rybkin told Interfax news agency that Yeltsin would meet Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov soon after officials completed documents charting a new relationship between Russia and the secessionist North Caucasus region. The two sides fought a 21-month war until last August.
Rybkin's deputy Boris Berezovsky told NTV television there had been progress in negotiations but only talks "in the near future" between the two leaders could settle the remaining issues.
Russia has beefed up security after two bomb explosions in the southern towns of Armavir and Pyatigorsk, both near Chechnya, killed four people.
The Chechen authorities issued an arrest warrant for radical Chechen commander Salman Raduyev, who had claimed responsibility for the attacks.
Rybkin said Yeltsin had agreed that a joint Russian-Chechen commission should investigate the blasts, which threatened to derail the difficult peace talks.
Raduyev, an isolated figure outside Chechnya's separatist leadership, has often vowed to attack Russian targets over Moscow's refusal to recognise Chechnya's independence.
